sharedText: that they should gather themselves together
reason: The highest-scoring candidate in the chapter, on a six-word run: the Lamanite king's proclamation that his people 'should gather themselves together again, to go to battle' against Ezra's proclamation that the children of the captivity 'should gather themselves together unto Jerusalem'. Both are proclamations and both use the KJV's reflexive of assembly, which the Book of Mormon uses hundreds of times. The window closes exactly where the two texts part — 'unto Jerusalem' against 'to go to battle against the Nephites' — and there is no other contact. The chapter's genuine Ezra-shaped material, a covenant enforced by penalty, is in the preceding chapter and is adjudicated at Alma 46:35 against 2 Chronicles 15.

sharedText: they would not obey the commandments of the king … the king was wroth
reason: Alma 47:2-3 stages the scene Esther 1 opens with: subjects refuse the king's command, and the king is angry at the disobedience. Esther 1:12 — 'the queen Vashti refused to come at the king's commandment … therefore was the king very wroth' — is the King James Bible's one such scene, and a reader who knows Esther will stop here. It will not carry a link. 'The king was wroth' as the Book of Mormon has it occurs in no KJV verse; 'was wroth' is spread over twenty-four; nothing else in the two passages agrees; and the Book of Mormon's refusers are an army afraid of dying, not a queen refusing to be displayed. Registered so the resemblance is on record as considered and declined.

sharedText: come down / four times after this sort
reason: The closest situational analogue in the King James Bible to Alma 47:10-13, and the one a reader is most likely to propose. Nehemiah's enemies invite him repeatedly to come down from his work to a meeting in the plain — 'but they thought to do me mischief' — he answers 'I cannot come down' twice in one verse, and Nehemiah 6:4 counts the sendings: 'yet they sent unto me four times after this sort'. Amalickiah likewise sends four times, likewise means mischief, and likewise cannot get his man to come down. The reason it is not the source is that the wording belongs to another passage: 'sent again the second time' is a KJV singleton at 2 Samuel 14:29, where Absalom is the sender and the refusal is verbatim, and the chapter's other borrowings (47:4, 47:30) come from the same three chapters of 2 Samuel. The link is written at 47:11 and a reader of Nehemiah 6 is sent there. Nehemiah's fourfold count remains the better explanation of why Amalickiah sends four times rather than Absalom's two, and it is recorded on that link.

A six-word run of pure connective tissue. The nobleman of Capernaum besought Jesus 'that he would come down, and heal his son'; Amalickiah sends a message 'desiring that he would come down, and that he would bring his guards with him'. Two indirect requests in the same English construction, sharing no content word but the verb of descent, which both texts need because both have a person higher up than another. 'Come down to' alone stands in eleven KJV verses. Nothing about Alma 47 touches the Capernaum healing.

sharedText: that he would suffer them to
reason: Tied for the chapter's top n-gram score, and worthless. Amalickiah's surrounded men 'plead with Amalickiah that he would suffer them to fall in with their brethren'; the Gadarene demons 'besought him that he would suffer them to enter into' the swine. The six shared words are the KJV's ordinary formula for a granted petition and the two petitions have nothing else in common. A clean instance of the trap at ADJUDICATING §4: a long run that means nothing on its own.

sharedText: the king assassinated by his own servants, who then flee
reason: Alma 47:24-30 turns on a story the Book of Mormon has Amalickiah fabricate — that the king's own servants stabbed him and fled — and the King James Bible tells that story three times: Rechab and Baanah kill Ishbosheth and escape (2 Samuel 4:5-7), Joash's servants make a conspiracy and slay him (2 Kings 12:20), Amon's servants conspire and slay the king in his own house (2 Kings 21:23). The Book of Mormon supplies no wording from any of them and, more tellingly, refuses the only idiom they share: the KJV kills kings by smiting them 'under the fifth rib', in four verses and always politically, while Alma 47:24 says 'stabbed the king to the heart' — a verb that appears in no KJV verse at all, in a sentence whose 'lying in his gore' uses a noun the KJV never uses. The scene is biblical and its language is not. The type-scene that does carry a link is the treacherous greeting of 2 Samuel 20:9-10, written at this verse.

sharedText: Whosoever loved the king, let him go forth
reason: 'Whosoever loved the king, let him go forth and pursue his servants' is a loyalty muster, and the KJV has two famous ones: Moses in the gate — 'Who is on the LORD's side? let him come unto me' (Exodus 32:26) — and Jehu at Jezreel's window, 'Who is on my side? who?' (2 Kings 9:32). Both are interrogatives answered by a gathering; Alma 47:27 is a relative clause followed by a jussive, shares no wording with either, and is a fraud rather than a test of allegiance. The resemblance is generic to the situation. Recorded because the cry is the kind of sentence a reader assumes must be quoted from somewhere.

'Took her unto him to wife' reproduces a phrase that occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 20:30 — 'and the second took her to wife, and he died childless' — the second of seven brothers in the Sadducees' levirate riddle about the resurrection. The rarity is real and the sense is unrelated: Luke's phrase is a legal obligation discharged in a hypothetical, Alma's is a usurper securing a crown. The figural link at this verse is written to 1 Kings 2:22, where the King James Bible states the convention Amalickiah is exploiting.

The machine's proposal at the verse where the true source is 2 Samuel 15:6. Joshua 7:5 is the rout at Ai: 'wherefore the hearts of the people melted, and became as water' — courage failing. Alma 47:30 is 'Amalickiah, by his fraud, gained the hearts of the people' — allegiance transferred. Same four words, opposite organ-metaphor; and the KJV's own phrase for what Amalickiah does, 'stole the hearts of the men of Israel', is a singleton one book later.
